job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In the quiet ponds of rural India, scientists are observing the fascinating life cycle of frogs. Unlike humans, who are viviparous and give birth to developed young, frogs lay eggs in water where external fertilisation occurs. This process is highly coordinated; the female releases eggs, and the male releases sperm into the water simultaneously, ensuring they meet. Once fertilised, the zygote is a single cell that begins to divide, eventually forming an embryo. This embryo does not feed on sperm; instead, it relies on nutrients stored within the egg itself. As the embryo develops into a tadpole, it undergoes metamorphosis, a dramatic transformation where the body shape changes completely rather than just growing larger. While reproduction is essential for the survival of the frog species, it is not required for an individual frog to stay alive. Interestingly, both sperm and eggs are specialized reproductive cells, just like any other cell in the body, despite their small size. Understanding these stages helps us appreciate how diverse life forms ensure their future generations survive through complex biological processes.

items.evidence: This process is highly coordinated; the female releases eggs, and the male releases sperm into the water simultaneously, ensuring they meet.
items.q: Why do male and female frogs release sperm and eggs into the water together?
options: So that sperm and eggs can meet
So that the female alone fertilises eggs
So that the young are born fully developed
So that eggs hatch as tiny adult frogs
items.explain: Both parents release eggs and sperm into water simultaneously so they meet and fertilisation happens.

wrong.why: thinks external fertilisation does not need both parents
mixes up frogs with viviparous animals like humans
thinks the new life already looks like the parent

items.evidence: This embryo does not feed on sperm; instead, it relies on nutrients stored within the egg itself.
items.q: A frog embryo grows inside its egg in a pond. Where does its food come from?
options: From nutrients kept inside the egg
From the sperm that fertilised the egg
From the pond water around the egg
From the mother frog's body directly
items.explain: The embryo does not feed on sperm; it uses nutrients stored within the egg itself.

wrong.why: thinks the embryo feeds on the father's sperm
picks the nearby detail that eggs are laid in water
thinks all young are fed inside the mother, as in humans

items.evidence: As the embryo develops into a tadpole, it undergoes metamorphosis, a dramatic transformation where the body shape changes completely rather than just growing larger.
items.q: A tadpole becomes a frog. Why is this called metamorphosis and not just growth?
options: Its whole body shape changes completely
It simply gets bigger in the same shape
It splits off from the parent like a bud
Its single cell divides into many cells
items.explain: Metamorphosis means the body shape changes completely, not just growing larger.

wrong.why: thinks metamorphosis just means growing bigger
mixes it up with the zygote dividing, an earlier stage

items.evidence: While reproduction is essential for the survival of the frog species, it is not required for an individual frog to stay alive.
items.q: A healthy frog never reproduces in its whole life. What happens to that frog?
options: It can still stay alive and healthy
It will die since it did not reproduce
Its frog species dies out right away
It will reproduce by budding instead
items.explain: Reproduction keeps the species going, but one frog does not need it to stay alive.

wrong.why: thinks an animal must reproduce to stay alive
confuses the individual frog with the whole species
thinks budding is a backup way frogs reproduce
